model_source.split_method: Deduplicated train texts of 8..50 whitespace words; shuffle each class with fixed seed; 64/class development, next 128/class selection. All official validation examples reserved for final evaluation.
model_source.limitations: Forced-choice sentiment, not free generation. Public dataset may have appeared in pretraining. Official validation serves as our final holdout, not the hidden GLUE test set. Train-derived selection can include related phrases.

candidates.hypothesis: Blending the positive and negative label rows with good and bad may align the classifier with evaluative sentiment rather than other meanings of polarity, correcting review-specific mistakes. Because embeddings are tied, this also changes those label tokens in the instruction.

Several positive reviews have small negative margins. Increasing only the positive row by one percent may correct a modest negative preference while preserving larger negative margins; this selective edit can change argmax, though tied input embeddings also affect contextual states.

The good/bad blend shifted many margins toward positive, improving positive examples but losing negatives. Retaining the semantic blend while increasing the negative row's original component from 0.75 to 0.78 should offset that preference and reveal whether the evaluative direction improves classification. Tied embeddings also change instruction representations.

The semantic blend corrected several positive reviews, but its unadjusted positive preference lost negatives; the 0.78 negative coefficient overcorrected and lost positives. An intermediate 0.765 coefficient should retain more semantic corrections while balancing the class margins. This changes both the tied output row and instruction embedding, so accuracy must be measured directly.

Candidate 3 improved development accuracy by 3.125 percentage points with lower label NLL. Increasing the good/bad semantic contribution from 25% to 50%, with a proportional negative-row correction, tests whether stronger evaluative sentiment alignment corrects additional mistakes. Because embeddings are tied, this also changes label representations in the instruction; the gain is uncertain and must be measured.

The 50% good/bad blend still favors positive predictions: several negative errors have margins below 0.2, while many corrected positives have larger margins. Raising the negative row's base coefficient from 0.53 to 0.54 should recover some negatives while preserving semantic corrections, potentially improving accuracy and NLL. Tied input embeddings also change, so this is an empirical test rather than a fixed logit adjustment.
